# Solvers

Some equations are implicit: the unknown appears on both sides, so the
value is approached by iteration rather than evaluated in one step. For
those, the scheme is part of the specification rather than an
implementation detail.

The reason is the agreement test. Two implementations running the same
scheme converge to the same value; two running different-but-equally-valid
schemes agree only to within their difference, which is far larger than
either declares as a tolerance. The cross-language check would then fail on
a disagreement about the solver rather than about the physics. Naming the
scheme in the spec is what makes the comparison mean something.

## Declared schemes

| Calculation | Kind | Tolerance | Convergence | Max iterations | Initial guess |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [`eos.pr_z_factor`](../eos/pr_z_factor.md) | `cubic_roots` | `1e-12` | `relative` | `50` | — |
| [`hydraulics.friction_factor_colebrook`](../hydraulics/friction_factor_colebrook.md) | `fixed_point` | `1e-12` | `relative` | `100` | `0.02` |

## Convergence

The stopping rule is applied to successive iterates `x_k`. The two rules are
not interchangeable - the same tolerance means different things under each,
which is why the spec names one explicitly:

- `relative`: `|x_(k+1) - x_k| <= tolerance * |x_(k+1)|`
- `absolute`: `|x_(k+1) - x_k| <= tolerance`

## Why the list is closed

The schema admits the schemes both implementations run, and no others. A
spec naming a scheme no implementation can run would describe a calculation
that exists only on paper, and would read as validation while doing nothing.
Widening the enum is a deliberate act that happens alongside the
implementation and its agreement test, never before it - which is how
`cubic_roots` arrived beside `fixed_point`, and why the table above lists
two rows rather than one.
